newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE cocoa futures stay lower by close.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE cocoa futures stay lower by close.

text.p: Origin selling on the back of renewed strength in sterling hammered London cocoa prices on Tuesday, traders said.
The market was earlier knocked lower by trade selling while grinder interest remained muted.
Origin selling was seen in forwards and in the nearbys, driving benchmark March to a low of 897 stg. The contract closed 11 stg lower at 901 stg.
Traders said players were also disappointed over the weakening market in New York.
"Some people thought stops would be touched when (London's) May went below 924 (stg) but that didn't happen," said one.
"I think people who are on the long side of the market are getting frustrated," the trader added.
News of a drop in weekly Ghanaian cocoa purchases had no immediate influence on prices.
Traders said the drop did not necessarily mean the crop is beginning to tail off. "People noticed the drop but they didn't see it as a bullish factor," one said.
Ghana cocoa purchases in the 14th week of the current 1996/97 season ending January 16 amounted to 15,614 tonnes, down from 16,364 tonnes in the previous week, the Ghana Cocoa Board said on Tuesday.
The latest figures compare with 8,798 tonnes in the corresponding period of 1995/96.

Earlier in the session, an International Cocoa Organization forecast of a deficit of 255,000 tonnes for 1996/97 failed to sway the market from the doldrums as it came in line with traders' expectations.
"They don't tend to come out with anything too outrageous and to be honest market sentiment tends to take what they say a little bit lightly," commented one trader.
Volume reached a very modest 4,893 lots.

March/May was static around 22-23 stg but traders noted a pick up in gradings could herald a reasonable delivery against spot although there was no indication the holder of large physical stocks would dump them.
The physical market continued to languish with traders desperately looking for signs that German industry is stepping up buying. But they appeared in no rush.
One trader said Germans refused to take up Ghana offers at level March, dashing hopes for a rise in business.
"They are only picking up scraps," he said, linking the lack of appetite to the mark's relative weakness.
